fields.Front: What are the three structural regions of the Internet named in the slides?
fields.Back: 1) Network edge: hosts (clients and servers, servers often in data centers). 2) Access networks and physical media: wired/wireless links. 3) Network core: interconnected routers, a network of networks.

fields.Front: What is an access network, and what is the first router called?
fields.Back: The network that physically connects an end system to the first router on a path toward any distant end system; that first router is the edge router.

fields.Front: What two questions should you keep in mind about any access network?
fields.Back: 1) What is its bandwidth / transmission rate (bits per second)? 2) Is access shared or dedicated among users?

fields.Front: Name the three categories of access networks in the slides.
fields.Back: Residential access networks, institutional access networks (school, company), and mobile access networks (WiFi, 4G/5G).

fields.Front: How does DSL reach the Internet, and what device terminates the line at the central office?
fields.Back: It uses the existing telephone line to the telco central office, where the DSLAM (DSL access multiplexer) separates data (sent to the Internet) from voice (sent to the telephone network).

fields.Text: DSL: {{c1::24-52 Mbps}} dedicated downstream and {{c2::3.5-16 Mbps}} dedicated upstream (slide figures).
fields.Extra: Asymmetric and dedicated (each home has its own line to the central office).

fields.Text: HFC = {{c1::hybrid fiber coax}}: fiber from the cable headend to neighbourhood junctions, coaxial cable to homes; cable Internet reuses the cable TV network.
Cable (HFC) access: up to {{c1::40 Mbps - 1.2 Gbps}} downstream and {{c2::30-100 Mbps}} upstream; the access network is {{c3::shared}} among homes on the way to the cable headend.
In cable access the {{c1::CMTS (cable modem termination system)}} at the headend plays the role the {{c2::DSLAM}} plays in DSL.

fields.Front: How do data and TV share the cable in cable-based access?
fields.Back: Frequency division multiplexing (FDM): different channels (video, data, control) are transmitted in different frequency bands on the same cable.

fields.Front: List the components of a typical home network shown on the slides.
fields.Back: Cable or DSL modem; router, firewall, NAT (often combined in one box); wired Ethernet (1 Gbps); WiFi wireless access point (54, 450 Mbps) serving wireless devices.

fields.Front: In a wireless access network, what is the base station also called?
fields.Back: An access point (AP). The shared wireless access network connects end systems to a router via the base station.

fields.Text: Wireless LANs (802.11b/g/n WiFi) operate within ~{{c1::100 ft}} of the access point at {{c2::11, 54, 450 Mbps}} transmission rates.
Wide-area cellular access: range of {{c1::tens of km}}, rates of {{c2::tens of Mbps}}, technologies {{c3::4G/5G}} (6G coming).
fields.Extra: Provided by a mobile/cellular network operator.

fields.Front: What rates do enterprise Ethernet and enterprise WiFi provide (slides)?
fields.Back: Ethernet wired access: 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps. WiFi access points: 11, 54, 450 Mbps.

fields.Front: Describe the host sending function in three steps.
fields.Back: 1) Take the application message. 2) Break it into smaller chunks called packets of length L bits. 3) Transmit each packet into the access network at transmission rate R (link capacity / bandwidth).

fields.Front: Which access technologies are SHARED and which are DEDICATED?
fields.Back: Shared: cable (HFC), WiFi, cellular. Dedicated: DSL, switched Ethernet ports (home or enterprise).
